talks.title: LayerOne 2026
talks.teaser: A demo party at the conference spotlights ANSI art, wildcard builds, and live performances on custom demoboard hardware.
talks.summary:
The session opens as an evening demo party, described as a hacker competition that mixes art, music, programming, and hardware. The host outlines three categories for the year: ANSI art, a returning wildcard class, and demoboard entries, with formal winners to be announced later.

In the ANSI segment, entries are shown in arbitrary order, mixing colorful text graphics with humor and references to BBS-era culture. Artists and groups are credited as each piece plays. Wildcard follows with Merlin’s presentation built in Jenga and Raylib, emphasizing card rendering and flip logic in a pinball-inspired style. Adam then demos a Layer One demoboard emulator created through an automated pipeline fed datasheets, schematics, and reference demos; it runs demos with sound and is published online, though timing and cycle accuracy still need tuning without hardware-in-the-loop feedback.

The demoboard block brings volunteers on stage for live runs, including freshly built work, soldering limitations that leave displays monochrome, meme and music-driven pieces, and code assisted by chat models. Organizers invite attendees to learn about the board the next day, note remaining kits for sale, and close toward dinner. For practitioners, the through-line is how a conference village compresses demoscene craft, embedded tinkering, and experimental tooling into a single communal showcase rather than a single research narrative.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - SPECTRA: Semantic Pattern Extraction for Scalable Malware Detection (Mohsen Ahmadi)
talks.teaser: Presents a semantic binary representation that matches malware variants at scale, between fragile and slow similarity methods.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles malware similarity at scale, meaning how closely samples from many variants and families relate. The speaker argues that common methods each give something up: byte and fuzzy hashes are fast but break on small changes, control-flow comparisons can be defeated by transformations such as control flow flattening, and behavioral traces can be evaded with delays or triggers. The presented system, Spectra, aims for a middle ground by building a semantic, genome-like vector for each binary that stays stable across variants. Its goals are determinism, architecture independence, scalability and machine learning compatibility.

The pipeline lifts machine code into VEX IR, chosen over LLVM because it works on raw binaries and exposes low-level operations. Each IR operation maps to a semantic category, which is counted per basic block and normalized into vectors. For strings, the speaker showed that greedy dictionary splitting and a probabilistic segmenter both stumble on identifiers such as a Linux syscall name, so a custom Word2Vec model was trained on reverse engineering artifacts. Inverse frequency weighting lets rare technical tokens count more than common boilerplate.

Binary ranking scores functions by how often the call graph reaches them and then weights their basic blocks, linking nearby strings such as socket or error messages to hot paths. The speaker noted the analysis relies on a fast static control-flow pass rather than symbolic or dynamic execution, so cases like C++ virtual calls can be missed. The takeaway is that IR-level semantics plus context-aware string embeddings can support similarity search across variants at scale, while the embedding component is open source and the rest of the system is proprietary.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - Vibes All the Way Down (Joe Rozner)
talks.teaser: A seasoned engineer recounts using coding agents to reverse ionCube loaders and build a working Flipper Zero EMV exploit via Proxmark.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker’s shift from AI skepticism to hands-on use of Claude Code for security work, framed against hype from model vendors and fear about skills becoming obsolete. The first case study revisits prior WorkTime spyware research where ionCube-protected PHP blocked full source recovery; an initial agent-assisted attempt peeled outer encryption and compression layers but stalled on bytecode access amid context rot, messy multi-binary analysis, and weak dynamic verification until later sessions with larger context, subagents, documented wikis, a headless Binary Ninja gRPC client, and Unicorn-backed checks eventually produced disassembly and a production-grade decompiler over several weeks at substantial token cost.

The second case study targets Flipper Zero wireless attack surface, focusing Unleashed firmware EMV parsing: a trivial unchecked memcopy yields stack overflow absent upstream. Claude helped rapidly craft a Proxmark-delivered proof of concept achieving program-counter control and a custom rop chain writing attacker text to flash; exploits were published while noting the bug remains in recent Unleashed builds with shifted gadgets. The speaker contrasts agent strengths—pattern matching on crypto constants, fast PoC iteration—with weaknesses such as hallucinated heap details, poor tool-failure awareness, and shaky exploitability judgment.

Closing lessons separate bug density from discovery depth, compare AI assistance to prior waves like fuzzing, and argue agents mostly widen the top of the vulnerability funnel rather than replacing skilled triage and remediation. Benchmark hype around end-to-end exploit chains is weighed against cost, maintainer-led findings in mature code like curl, and the limited share of the lifecycle that automated discovery actually covers.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - The History of Malware (Eliad Kimhy)
talks.teaser: Follows malware from 1980s floppy-disk viruses through macro worms and botnets to modern ransomware, highlighting recurring patterns.
talks.summary:
The talk traces roughly four decades of malware and argues that the technology changes while the motives and patterns repeat. It opens with the 1989 AIDS Trojan, distributed on floppy disks by mail, which encrypted file names and demanded payment, and presents it as an early form of ransomware. From there it covers the early 1980s, when viruses were mostly experimental pranks passed along on physical media, and the mid-1980s shift in public awareness after readers wrote in about real infections.

The middle section follows the move from playful code to destructive code. Examples include Elk Cloner on Apple computers, the Brain virus traced to Pakistan, and timed payloads such as Jerusalem that caused recurring panics. After Windows 95 and Office 95 arrived, macro viruses spread quickly and displaced DOS viruses, and Melissa and ILOVEYOU showed how email turned them into worms. Trojans such as NetBus, Back Orifice and SubSeven then used IRC as a command channel, which laid groundwork for botnets.

In the 2010s, cryptocurrency made payments harder to trace, and exploits such as EternalBlue and WannaCry enabled large outbreaks. Botnet operators began adding ransomware to the end of their attack chains, as with Gameover Zeus. The talk closes with today's info stealers and initial access brokers, then questions how AI tools will shape security, arguing that the outcome is not yet clear.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - Busting Black Basta Exploiting Ransomware (Tobias Mueller)
talks.teaser: Explains Black Basta's repeated-keystream bug for file recovery and a novel SSH systemd trick to reach their infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how ransomware gangs pressure victims through encryption, data theft, and dark-web shaming, then focuses on Black Basta’s prominence, its ESXi targeting, and a 2022 cryptography change that introduced a serious implementation flaw.

After walking through partial-file encryption patterns, the presenter shows how reusing one XChaCha20 keystream block across chunks breaks confidentiality when attackers know—or can infer—64 plaintext bytes. Sparse virtual disk images with large zero regions made widespread recovery practical on ESXi estates, outpacing the crew’s own multi-threaded decryptor. The talk covers building a decryptor from reversed Linux binaries, choices around public release versus victim outreach, and context from leaked operator chat.

It closes with defensive lessons—phishing entry points, backup isolation, restore drills—and a separate incident-response angle: SSH port forwarding into attacker infrastructure, including using forwarded systemd Unix sockets to run commands despite restricted authorized_keys, surfacing live victim tunnels until the gang vanished.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - Pulverize Chips with a Squib in the Heatsink (Mehmet Sencan)
talks.teaser: Covers trial-and-error destruction of GPUs with explosives as a tamper response, and the licensing needed to do it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from supply-chain trust and physical attacks on hardware. The speaker points to recent work that images secure chips, reads plaintext from an FPGA at runtime, and glitches satellite receivers. The proposed defense is to seal hardware inside a tamper perimeter with sensors, so that a break-in or a low battery triggers destruction of the chip.

The speaker reviews destruction options such as EMP, chemicals, electrical zapping and zeroization, then reports his own trials. Nanothermite did not shatter chips, even on a GPU under a heat sink. A number six detonator and a detonating cord destroyed GPUs but caused too much damage and scattering. Smaller pyrotechnic initiators, including a NASA-standard initiator and micro squibs, destroyed chips with far less blast. An oscilloscope trace showed the firing event lasting about 50 microseconds.

The second half covers the regulatory path. The Department of Transportation classifies energetic materials for shipping, and the ATF requires a federal explosives license for commercial use or storage, with approved magazines and local fire departments that vary in their rules. Some pyrotechnic parts can ship on passenger aircraft without a license. The speaker suggests that a DOT classification and an ATF exemption could let a tamper-destroying product be sold to end users, and he expects small companies could build such products within about a year.

talks.title: LayerOne 2026 - RedTeam 2026: Initial Access in Modern Environments (Adrian Novoa)
talks.teaser: Surveys initial access methods that evade modern Windows and cloud defenses, from Mark of the Web gaps to device code phishing.
talks.summary:
Adrian Novoa, a red team operator, covers how initial access has become harder as EDR, behavioral detection, email filtering and Microsoft's default hardening block the simple one-click payload. The talk focuses on file formats, identity and phishing angles that can still get a foothold.

The first part looks at Mark of the Web, the zone identifier Windows attaches to downloaded files. Container formats such as ISOs have historically hidden files from it, and WinRAR's default associations do not pass the tag on to XLL Excel plugins. Macros blocked for internet files were still open in Publisher, which Microsoft's policy omitted. Other vectors include WSL-launched ELF payloads, MSC files that run commands through URI handling, and VSIX extensions hidden inside OneNote files. Once a foothold exists, the speaker contrasts classic Impacket methods such as SMBExec, ATExec and Evil-WinRM with custom RDP-based and registry-based execution tools that avoid dropping binaries.

For cloud-connected targets, device code phishing abuses the OAuth device authorization flow to obtain tokens that are already MFA-authenticated, and a token with SharePoint or OneDrive access can upload files that carry no Mark of the Web. The talk also covers VPN phishing, where a native Windows VPN profile needs admin rights and a private network setting, and primary refresh token theft as a route to internal access. The closing point is that legitimate administrative behaviour is the hardest pattern to detect, and that the gap between defender expectations and attacker capability is where access is found.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023
talks.teaser: A conference demo party stacks tight PIC24 hardware with CHIP-8, fractal, and audio demos on one shared custom board.
talks.summary:
The session opens on LayerOne’s long-running demo-party tradition: a custom PCB built around a PIC24F running at 16 MHz with 96 KB of RAM and 256 KB of ROM, described as roughly akin to a 286 without floating point. Projector output and VGA signal tricks matter because older projectors tolerate the manipulations modern units block. Parts cost about thirteen dollars apiece amid chip shortages, and boot or toolchain snags are part of the show.

Competitors iterate on small, constraint-heavy programs. One entrant emulates CHIP-8 twice and runs two ROMs at once after fighting IDE and compiler version issues. Miss papaya shows an unfinished Mandelbrot fractal in BASIC on the PIC24, with an interactive shell for on-the-fly coding. Sick P’s “sick Mach 1” leans on most of the flash, drops MPLAB debug niceties, and pairs byte-beat drum patterns and macros; the host reads his script when he stays offstage.

The through-line is demoscene craft under severe limits rather than exploitation or defense. Practitioners take away how abstraction layers, flash budgets, and live hardware quirks shape what “done” means when every demo is arguably unfinished and the crowd commits to pushing the board further next year.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - ESXicution (z0rro & museifu)
talks.teaser: Outlines ESXi internals and public implants, then shows persistence, HTTP-tunneled C2, console hijacking, and snapshot secrets.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame the session as operating-system-level persistence and command-and-control on VMware ESXi after an attacker already has access. They explicitly exclude CVE-based exploits, initial compromise, vCenter, and guest-to-host escapes, then walk through ESXi as a type-1 hypervisor: the VMkernel microkernel, ramdisk-backed visorfs tarballs, vfat boot banks, vmfs for virtual disks, the reverse HTTP proxy to local sockets, BusyBox userland, and locked-down firewall defaults.

They survey publicly discussed implant families from 2022—including VirtualPeta, VirtualPie, and ESXiArgs—highlighting bind shells, log suppression, guest command execution, and crude ransomware behavior against VM disks. Deployment paths cover legacy community VIB force-install tricks (tightened in ESXi 8), SSH, and repackaging running-config archives so a custom tarball overlays filesystem state after maintenance mode. They add evasion such as briefly pausing syslog, hiding SSH and shared-console UI warnings via on-host HTML and JavaScript changes, and porting common Linux persistence (rc.local, cron, backdoored binaries, boot-bank modules, SSH authorized keys).

New tooling demos include SOCKS encapsulated in allowed HTTP admin traffic, pieshell-style execution through the proxy, console-session ticket theft for interactive shoulder-surfing, harvesting Kerberos ticket-granting tickets when the host is domain-joined, web-login keylogging, and LSASS extraction from VM snapshots converted with vmss2core—activity they argue sits below guest EDR visibility. They close without a formal ATT&CK walkthrough and take questions on VIB acceptance levels and hardening.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - Jurassic Passwords: No Thesaurus Necessary (Davie)
talks.teaser: Analyzes the word lists behind a kids' password generator and shows how quickly its output can be cracked.
talks.summary:
This talk takes a close look at Dinopass, a free online password generator marketed as easy for kids to remember. The speaker, a network engineer, scraped the site's simple-password API for about two weeks and gathered roughly 3.5 million results, of which only about 2.2 million were unique. Frequency analysis showed that the adjective "cute" appeared roughly twice as often as any other adjective, that only 89 two-digit endings occurred with 69 absent, and that 99 showed up about twice as often as the other endings.

Each generated password is an adjective, a noun and two digits, which yields about 3.3 million combinations. The speaker put that in context by comparing it with fully random passwords of four to five characters, then cracked sample hashes with John the Ripper and hashcat using only that word list and no rules. Six md5crypt accounts fell in under two minutes on an old laptop without a GPU, 100 NTLM hashes cracked in one second, and a set of 100 sha512crypt passwords took 24 minutes. The strong-password button adds capitalization and look-alike symbol swaps, which the speaker estimated only modestly widens the search space.

The speaker concludes that the word list is too small and the format too predictable to resist a targeted attack, and that the strong option does not change this much. Dinopass might suit a low-stakes login a child needs to type, but it should not protect shared lab systems, work accounts, or anything whose hashes could leak through backups, configuration files or web directory password files. The practical advice is to use a password manager to generate and store unique random passwords, and to enable two-factor authentication on important accounts.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - Flipper Zero: Annoying Tesla Owners Since 2021 (cesi0)
talks.teaser: A practitioner-oriented tour of Flipper Zero firmware forks, companion apps, and hands-on RF, NFC, infrared, and Bad USB use cases.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with what the Flipper Zero is: a portable, open-source gadget built around sub-gigahertz radio, NFC and RFID, infrared, GPIO expansion, and USB Bad HID payloads, plus how official firmware differs from community forks such as Unleashed, Rogue Master, and Flipper Extreme on rolling codes, frequency limits, and extra applications.

The middle walks through day-to-day operation: installing firmware via Q Flipper, mobile tools, and Flipper Labs; running Bad USB scripts (including tricks to mimic trusted keyboards); learning and replaying infrared remotes; sniffing, saving, and retransmitting sub-gigahertz signals, including unencrypted Tesla charge-port openers, raw captures for rolling protocols, frequency hopping workflows, and shortened brute-force sets for some garage-door code spaces. NFC and low-frequency RFID segments cover reading cards, dictionary and MFKey-style attacks against weak MIFARE setups, rapid cloning during assessments, and RFID fuzzing to probe higher-privilege badge values.

GPIO add-ons, public signal libraries, and active Discord/GitHub communities round out the picture. The speaker stresses lawful research only while showing how inexpensive replay and cloning make many consumer wireless and badge systems easy to abuse in the field.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - Eye Feel Fine: Modern Smart Camera Security (wasabi)
talks.teaser: Traces how smart camera security went wrong, from exposed streams to one vendor's cloud flaws, with practical advice for buyers.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how consumer and commercial security cameras evolved, from early D-Link devices built on ActiveX and Java applets to Foscam models with fixed root passwords, authentication bypasses and a hidden telnet enabler. Many vendors rely on the same off-the-shelf chipsets and vendor SDKs, so old kernels and firmware get reused across products and brands. Internet search results for exposed cameras, with default credentials, show how public access turns a device weakness into a privacy problem.

The middle section turns to cloud-connected cameras. One vendor left a known vulnerability unpatched for three years and removed a local RTSP feature from its firmware. The main case study covers a camera company's portal, where stream URLs were built from a serial number and a short random token that the server did not properly validate. The speaker shows that the token could be widened to 16 bytes but the structure stayed guessable, and that a debugger block copied from a public forum could be bypassed. A reset option could also erase footage. The vendor's responses were slow, because reports went through tier-one support and translation gaps delayed fixes.

The closing advice is for both sides. Companies should work directly with researchers, avoid threats and communicate clearly. Buyers should treat outdoor camera feeds as public, keep home cameras on isolated networks, and consider a local, open-source recorder such as Frigate instead of relying on the cloud.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - DNS DriveBy: Stealthy GPS Tracking Using Open Wi-Fi (Alyx Lynd)
talks.teaser: Shows how a cheap Wi-Fi microcontroller can track a car's GPS route by leaking data through DNS requests on open networks.
talks.summary:
Alex Lynd presents DNS drive-by, a name he coined for a war driving technique that sends reconnaissance or GPS data out through open, unauthenticated Wi-Fi networks. The idea is a low-cost alternative to a cellular module or SIM card for tracking devices. He frames it as a proof of concept built on others' earlier work.

The prototype is a small board built around an ESP8266-class Wi-Fi microcontroller with a GPS module, a battery and a 3D-printed case, with a total build cost stated as around ten dollars. A vibration sensor wakes it from deep sleep when the car moves. Captive portals block ordinary web traffic, but plain HTTP redirects and firewall rules still let DNS queries through. The payload encodes coordinates in base32 and sends them as subdomains of a Canary Tokens DNS endpoint, so the operator downloads a log of requests and plots the route in Google My Maps. A test on a friend's car produced a route with stops at a shopping center and a cemetery. In a side comparison, an LTE tracker updated most consistently, a Tile tracker updated intermittently and AirTags produced a single update.

The takeaway is that cheap microcontrollers can support credible reconnaissance and tracking, and that a one-way DNS channel needs no full internet session. He closes by pointing to the privacy risks of cheap trackers and to microcontrollers as an accessible starting point for beginners in security research.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - Interpret This! Hunting for Bugs in the Python Interpreter (Nathaniel Singer)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of CPython architecture and three unpatched production bugs, plus a practical strategy for hunting interpreter flaws.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a high-level tour of CPython: source becomes an abstract syntax tree, then bytecode, then CPU execution, alongside Micropython, Jython, and other implementations. It frames the PSF maintenance burden, what counts as in-scope (interpreter, native libraries, and pip), and how sensitive fixes flow through the security response team versus ordinary pull requests.

The middle section turns to a repeatable research strategy—threat modeling from input through cache and execution, mining open issues and pull requests, reading developer comments, and optional static analysis. Three findings illustrate the approach. A bytecode cache poisoning issue abuses timestamp-only validation in `.pyc` headers so malicious bytecode can run while source appears unchanged, with cross-user impact on shared installs and a reported CVSS score of 8.4. A stable ABI bug triggers an unchecked overflow in native array copying that can crash the whole interpreter process. A pip typo-squatting demonstration wraps a legitimate imaging library around a trivial reverse shell that still passes upload checks.

Closing guidance stresses deep product comprehension, light threat modeling, and chasing high-impact surfaces such as networking libraries. The speaker notes limited PSRT bandwidth, hard tradeoffs for cache integrity fixes, and speculative use of language models to flag near-duplicate or obviously malicious packages.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - Intro to Memory Corruption and ROP (Jon King (jk))
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding LayerOne 2023 - Intro to Memory Corruption and ROP (Jon King (jk)).
talks.summary:
Jon King presents a practical, real-time walkthrough of solving a binary exploitation CTF challenge called 'EasyWeb' (300 points). He demonstrates the complete workflow for exploiting a buffer overflow vulnerability in a web server binary running on port 8080.

The speaker begins with reconnaissance techniques—running the binary, analyzing its strings, and using checksec to identify security mitigations (stack canaries, NX, ASLR). He then sends malformed HTTP requests to trigger a segmentation fault, confirming a buffer overflow in the process_client function.

Using GDB integrated with pwntools (a Python exploitation library), he analyzes the crash to gain control of the return pointer by carefully crafting payloads. Since NX prevents executing injected shellcode, he pivots to Return-Oriented Programming (ROP)—chaining existing code fragments called gadgets to accomplish tasks.

The core technique demonstrated is ret2csu, a powerful ROP method using the __libc_csu_init function present in historically-compiled glibc binaries. This allows controlled function calls with arbitrary arguments. To bypass ASLR (which randomizes libc addresses), King constructs a ROP chain calling write() to leak a GOT entry address back to the attacker through the socket. By calculating the offset between this leaked address and known values, the attacker can determine libc's base address and access all needed functions.

The walkthrough uses Ghidra for binary analysis, ROPgadget for gadget discovery, and demonstrates x86-64 calling conventions (RDI, RSI, RDX for first three arguments). The speaker notes that ret2csu is becoming obsolete in Ubuntu 22.04 and later. Due to time constraints, the full exploitation chain remains incomplete, but the foundational techniques for bypassing modern mitigations are clearly demonstrated.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023 - My Laptop Dreams of Polydactyl Sheep (machinist)
talks.teaser: A hands-on tour of local Stable Diffusion demos, prompt craft, and why synthetic media erodes visual trust.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames Stable Diffusion as a black-box system worth probing without deep math: a modest laptop with about eight gigabytes of VRAM can run a local Python stack and generate images from text, refine existing pictures, upscale small outputs, and extend scenes through outpainting. The speaker walks through Automatic1111 in the browser, audience-sourced prompts, batching many candidates because most outputs fail, and knobs such as sampling steps, CFG scale, seeds, and negative prompts to steer style while avoiding common artifacts like extra fingers, bad teeth, and gibberish lettering embedded in PNG metadata.

Live runs include whimsical subjects, horror-manga styling, upscaling pitfalls at four-k and eight-k resolutions, and image-to-image iteration that slowly emphasizes desired details. Highlights also cover community tricks—emphasis syntax, inverted CFG behavior, and the limits of fixing limb distortions tied to training data. The talk contrasts local airplane-mode generation with hosted services and notes how quickly quality jumped from unusable cloud experiments to convincing results.

Closing themes stress societal impact: deepfake ads, plausibly deniable fabricated scenes, and the need for skeptical viewing habits. The speaker argues the tooling removes tedious graphic busywork rather than replacing human taste, while experience teaches when to stop tuning prompts. Practitioners leave with practical prompting habits, awareness of failure modes, and a sober view of eroding trust in visual evidence.

talks.title: LayerOne 2023
talks.teaser: A double-elimination robot sumo tournament pits homemade bots in 60-second matches until winners emerge by knockout or applause.
talks.summary:
The session is a live Hebocon-style robot sumo tournament at LayerOne. The host lays out the rules before the bracket begins: competitors must make contact for a bout to count, each pairing gets up to three tries, rounds run 60 seconds, and the format is double elimination or as close as organizers can manage. When neither machine shows translational movement, the crowd may decide the outcome by applause, with cameras pointed at the ring so the audience can follow the action.

Named entries such as Shake It Ralph, Twisted Croc, Kill Dozer, Toolkit of Mass Destruction, and Man's Search for Meaning trade wins and losses through winners and losers brackets. Many bouts need rematches for missed contact; some robots spray paint, wield improvised gear, or stall until time runs out. Late rounds push familiar names toward the top, including Twisted Croc versus Toolkit of Mass Destruction for placement, with first through third receiving trophies or first pick of prizes.

Practitioners attending for security content should treat this as conference community programming: improvised hardware, betting jokes, and audience participation rather than defensive or offensive tradecraft. The takeaway is how a hacker con hosts low-cost maker competition alongside its main tracks.

talks.title: LayerOne 2021 - Chloe Messdaghi
talks.teaser: Argues that media stereotypes and outdated laws leave hackers unprotected, and shows how disclosure policies build trust.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that hackers lack legal protection and are widely seen as criminals. The speaker separates a hacker, who stays in scope and works with permission to keep systems secure, from an attacker, who exploits systems for gain. She recounts a researcher who declined a 30k payout from an in-house DJI bug bounty because the required contract gave him no protection. The company then threatened a lawsuit under the CFAA, and he published the exchange in a blog post.

Media imagery and loose terminology shape public perception, and that perception feeds into organizations and legislation. Attendees are encouraged to politely correct journalists and marketing teams, and a group sent a letter to the New York Times copy desk about using "hacker" for attackers. Figures cited include 94 percent of Forbes Global 2000 companies lacking vulnerability disclosure policies and one in four hackers never reporting what they find. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, largely unchanged since the 1980s, is described as vague and open to stacked charges. The Aaron Swartz case, with 17 months of legal battle, 35 years of possible prison time and 1 million in fines, shows the cost. Aaron's Law, meant to fix these problems, never passed.

The practical close covers writing disclosure policies in plain language that state scope, contacts and response expectations, and using a platform or resources such as disclose.io if needed. Listeners can contact their representatives, vote, share personal hacker stories, and support groups such as the EFF and CERT/CC. The core message is that change starts with individuals.

talks.title: LayerOne 2021 - Wasabi - WMI Stole Your Cat
talks.teaser: Walks defenders through Windows Management Instrumentation, showing how it is misused for persistence and how to detect it.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at Windows Management Instrumentation, a built-in Windows component that can be queried locally or over the network by anyone holding valid credentials. The speaker argues that defenders often have little visibility into WMI because it is not a service they consciously run, and aims to help them understand how it is used and misused using tools that already exist on Windows. The background covers its namespaces and sub-objects, its SQL-like query syntax, its link to PowerShell, and the legacy wmic command.

The middle of the talk is a hands-on tour. The speaker queries processes and services, and shows that a remote operator can stop and disable a service through WMI. The Security Center endpoint is used to see which antivirus product is registered, and the speaker demonstrates how Defender exclusions and real-time monitoring settings can be changed through the same interface. Persistence is covered through the filter, consumer and binding components, including managed object files compiled into the object store, and the speaker explains where these subscriptions can be found and how a matching query can be used to remove them.

The closing section focuses on detection and hardening. Default event logs give little detail, and WMI tracing rolls over quickly, so the speaker recommends Sysmon to record when filters and consumers are created. The practical takeaways are to turn off scripting and WMI features that are not needed, restrict who can use WMI remotely through its permission settings, and use AppLocker to limit what can run on a system.

talks.title: LayerOne 2021 - Viss - How to Vet Your Vendors
talks.teaser: Shows how to judge a vendor's security from its public footprint before trusting it with your data.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the usual vendor risk process, where companies send a questionnaire and accept the answers, gives little real security assurance. The speaker, Viss, proposes that staff with some offensive skills check a prospective vendor's public footprint themselves before signing. The aim is not a full penetration test but a read on patterns of behavior that shows how the vendor runs its technology.

The method starts with easy checks: news coverage, the company's official social media accounts, public posts from employees, and leak databases. It then moves to the exposed perimeter, looking for old unpatched appliances, leaked certificates, dev and staging servers on the internet, internal hosts reachable from outside, and private addresses published in public DNS. Each finding is treated as a clue about how seriously the vendor handles its own security. Examples include a camera maker whose internet-facing Jenkins console was enough to start a wider compromise, and a misconfigured proxy that could reach a military network from the internet.

The talk closes by turning those findings into a threat model for the vendor relationship. That means asking what data the vendor would hold, what an insider or a compromise could do, and whether disaster recovery and crisis plans would hold up. Tabletop exercises and red-versus-blue scenarios are suggested as ways to test those plans. The practical takeaway is a dossier that lets decision makers avoid surprises before onboarding a vendor.

talks.title: LayerOne 2021 - Jos Weyers - How to Lose Your Keys in 2 Easy Steps
talks.teaser: Shows how a single photo of a key can be turned into a working copy, using cheap blanks and public cases.
talks.summary:
Jos Weyers sets out how keys can be lost in two steps: first a photo of a key is taken, then a copy is made from it. The speaker explains that a key's profile can be measured from a picture when a coin of known size sits beside it as a scale, and that software can analyse the key's depth and shape to work out the cuts. Blanks are then milled on a CNC machine or printed, so the copy can operate the lock.

The middle of the talk walks through real-world cases. The speaker describes a speed camera control cabinet in Belgium that a small key reportedly opened, with the cost given as 14 euros and 23 cents. Other examples involve fire service key boxes whose master keys appeared for sale online, and people who posted photos of their keys and homes on social media, where those pictures could be combined with street-level imagery. Each case is shown as a separate example of how a key or lock was exposed.

The talk closes with the point that a key is only as secure as the information about it. The speaker stresses that photos of keys, the way key services verify orders, and the handling of lock information deserve attention from anyone who relies on physical locks.

talks.teaser: Western Regional CCDC rebuilding delivers documentation, Triassic Land scenarios, Montreal hosting, and volunteer automation lessons.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe taking over black team for the Western Regional Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition after prior organizers stopped communicating and they lost hardware access. They frame competition work as mostly logistics—documentation, validation, meetings, and cost control—not merely writing challenge VMs. Teams behave like customers with rising expectations, while volunteers remain the least reliable component despite automation.

They rebuilt rules and documentation, shifted emphasis back toward cybersecurity rather than pure business tasks, and spent a year constructing a fictional company called Triassic Land with dozens of machines, domain users, custom ICS elements, and preparatory hints for students. Hosting moved away from expensive public cloud dev cycles toward dedicated OVH servers in Montreal, hybrid VPN links between per-team company environments, and painful lessons when a hypervisor failed mid-qualifier.

The second speaker details invitationals as a pipeline to retain builders, mentoring for volunteers, Discord bots for operations, and aspirations to standardize vulnerable deployments with playbooks and more load testing. They close by soliciting volunteers and arguing that pairing training with competition testing beats static awareness programs for many audiences.

talks.title: LayerOne 2019 - Let's Talk about WAF Bypass Baby (Brett "securitypanda" Gravois)
talks.teaser: Shows how HTTP/2 can route around WAF inspection by downgrading traffic through local proxies, with defensive tips for teams.
talks.summary:
Brett Gravois argues that few security researchers test HTTP/2, even though the protocol was published in 2015 and is now used by large sites. He covers its binary framing, multiplexed streams, header compression and server push, and the two forms it takes: a cleartext upgrade from HTTP/1.1 and a TLS-negotiated version using ALPN. He points out that many CDNs and load balancers appear to support HTTP/2 at the edge while the real connection is downgraded further along. He recommends the ng HTTP2 tooling, which walks through the full connection and shows the protocol actually negotiated.

The core of the talk is a way to test through a proxy that does not speak HTTP/2. Burp Suite is one such tool, so he sets up two local ng HTTP2 proxy instances. The first converts browser HTTP/2 traffic into HTTP/1.1 for Burp, and the second converts Burp's HTTP/1.1 back into HTTP/2 toward the server. The setup uses a self-signed certificate and a hosts entry that points a test site at localhost. He notes that results vary by target: some sites drop requests, some connect, and some show nothing. He argues that to network defenders the traffic looks like ordinary encrypted web traffic, so it can pass inspection that does not decrypt it. He also notes that this setup ties the proxy to a single site per connection.

He closes with defensive advice. If HTTP/2 is not needed, turn it off. If it is needed, confirm that the load balancer or vendor supports it properly. He points to a community list of known HTTP/2 implementations and to the RFC's security considerations section as useful references.

talks.title: LayerOne 2019 - Tales of the Lockpick Village (Marcus Richerson)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of conference lockpick villages, bypass methods, and practical defenses for doors, locks, and vehicles.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames lockpick villages as hands-on bridges into security culture, drawing on years of hosting events from small conference tables to crowds of hundreds at STEAM fairs. The speaker describes how teaching evolved from tables full of unexplained locks toward step-by-step coaching and a difficulty ladder—from handcuffs and shims through clear pin tumblers, spool pins, and higher-security brands.

The middle of the session catalogs non-destructive defeat techniques: single-pin picking, raking, bumping, wafer and tubular locks, warded bypass, combination decoding, latch sliding, under-door tools, impressioning, and vehicle entry with wedges and reach tools. Semi-destructive and destructive options appear alongside improvised “MacGyver” approaches using clips, shoelaces, and cans. Conference CTF scoreboards and anecdotes illustrate how digital and physical challenge tracks mix.

The close emphasizes defenses—quality locks, latch fit, RFID hardening, window film, safes, alarms, and layered barriers—and points newcomers to common learning resources. The takeaway is that many everyday physical controls fail quickly once mechanisms are understood, while villages offer a structured, low-pressure place to learn that reality firsthand.

talks.title: LayerOne 2019 - The SEArt of War: The CHIMAERA Threat Model (Christina Lekat & Tigran Terpandjan)
talks.teaser: Introduces the CHIMAERA model for blending culture, history, and asymmetry into adversary-focused red team exercises.
talks.summary:
The presenters introduce CHIMAERA, a threat-modeling framework shaped by a year and a half of research and named after a Star Wars analogy to Grand Admiral Thrawn’s habit of studying adversaries through tactics, history, philosophy, and art. They argue that red teaming in industry overweights technical TTP replay while threat intelligence often sits apart from adversarial operations, and that both need the same analytical depth.

The framework is split into analytical and practical halves. Analytical modules cover culture (including PMESII-style political, military, economic, social, and information context), history and behavioral predictability, intelligence collection and bias control, and criminal-style profiling from circumstantial evidence. Case studies such as Mia Ash and APT reporting illustrate how history, targeting patterns, and social engineering align with attribution and industry relevance. The practical side stresses asymmetry—stacking unrelated advantages—emulation versus shallow simulation, tailoring scenarios to the client’s sector, and considering physical, social, and digital attack surfaces together.

The session closes with an audience walkthrough applying the modules to Mandiant’s APT1 profile and summarized takeaways: pair technical red teaming with analytic tradecraft, remember human actors behind groups, get comfortable with unfamiliar disciplines, and keep threat intelligence and red teams working as one loop.

talks.title: LayerOne 2019 - Swords to Plowshares: Repurposing the Ghost Gunner (Machinist)
talks.teaser: Shows how to operate the Ghost Gunner mill as a general-purpose CNC machine, from homing and G-code to coordinate setup.
talks.summary:
The speaker examines the Ghost Gunner, a benchtop CNC mill built to finish 80% AR-15 lower receivers, and argues it can be run as a general-purpose machine. He explains the build choices that matter for milling: a heavy frame with linear rails, ball screws that remove backlash and allow climb cutting, and a brushless spindle on a cartridge bearing. He also notes that the stepper motors run open-loop, so an overly heavy cut can lose steps and shift the work.

Next comes the controller, which fits on an Arduino-class board and processes motion locally. He covers G-code modal groups, absolute versus incremental positioning, and setting a work coordinate system with G54. Operating limits get heavy attention: the spindle has a 3 to 10,000 rpm range and 125 watts maximum, and the firmware has no soft limits, so a bad command can drive an axis past its travel. Homing must run before the machine responds, and the table sits parallel to the spindle, which calls for a secondary fixture. He demonstrates jogging over a serial console and a G-code sender, and how to fix a program that uses negative coordinates.

The closing section covers diagnostics and risk. A healthy machine sounds like steady white noise, while clicking or straining points to lost steps or a jam. Stepper step rates can also produce audible tones, so he converts a MIDI file into G-code that plays a tune on the machine. He warns that G-code macro features can be used for much more harmful actions, so practitioners should confirm a machine's parameters before running code from an outside source.

talks.title: LayerOne 2019 - Hashes to Ashes: The Life & Times of Clandestine Infrastructure (Jason Kichen)
talks.teaser: Explores how nation-state and red-team operators design layered proxy networks to evade attribution and sustain access at scale.
talks.summary:
The presentation defines clandestine infrastructure as every system an attacker owns or controls between their workstation and the target, chiefly to move traffic while avoiding detection and especially attribution. It contrasts Hollywood remote-access myths with cases that demand physical proximity or trusted humans, then layers diagrams from a single redirector through split command-and-control and exfiltration paths, cellular devices, Wi-Fi gear, and separate phishing or exploitation stacks linked by long-term planning.

A fictional planning thread against a Peruvian weapons manufacturer illustrates how counterintelligence stakes, tool equities, and in-country helpers drive choices to buy, lease, cloud-host, or compromise relays, and how dedicated teams provision, test, and hand infrastructure to operators. Operations and maintenance emerge as the fragile center: keeping nodes alive across geopolitical shocks, pre-stocking capacity for many simultaneous missions, and unconscious patterns such as themed domain registrations that analysts can fuse into clusters.

When one element is burned, actors must walk compromise outward through shared payments, IDs, implants, and providers—a gamble with no fixed rulebook. The VPN Filter case shows routers used as global relay stock with a remote wipe suited to destroying nodes quickly, while a SOC anecdote stresses that blocking one channel may leave parallel egress intact. Defenders are urged to expect multiple paths, including people and phones, not a single malware callback.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018
talks.teaser: Shows how misconfigured Tor hidden services leak clearnet addresses, from server status pages to reused SSH keys.
talks.summary:
The talk gives a high-level recap of how Tor works, covering three-hop circuits with layered encryption, and how hidden services publish descriptors so clients can reach them through introduction and rendezvous points. It then moves from the routing itself to the ways hidden services are commonly exposed through their own configuration.

The speaker gathered onion addresses from paste sites and by recursively crawling the services he found, and described how operators of the distributed hash table can collect descriptors. Several misconfigurations are walked through. Apache server-status pages were reachable through a hidden service, and the default Ubuntu package enables that page, which exposed requests containing clearnet hostnames. A default virtual host answered requests with no Host header and returned a clearnet domain. SSH host key fingerprints matched clearnet servers when searched on Shodan. Private keys were left in web-accessible directories, and debug pages such as info.php listed public IP addresses.

A live scan of a list of onion addresses checked for these issues and took a few minutes to run. It produced results for a dozen or so hidden services. The main takeaway is to audit web servers, SSH and debugging interfaces for reused clearnet identifiers, and to verify every finding before trusting it.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - Data Security: How to Avoid an Embarrasing Breach (Matt Hoy)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding LayerOne 2018 - Data Security: How to Avoid an Embarrasing Breach (Matt Hoy).
talks.summary:
### Overview
At LayerOne 2018, speaker Matt Hoy presents an unconstrained, vendor-neutral perspective on data security, focusing on how organizations can prevent embarrassing data breaches. Drawing on his consulting and incident response background, Hoy argues that while incident response is often a losing battle, data security is an area where organizations have the agency to control their own environment. The presentation explores the historical evolution of data controls, identifies critical gaps in contemporary cloud data security lifecycles, and outlines practical strategies across people, processes, and technologies to track and protect critical data assets.

### Key Topics
- **Historical Evolution & Security Models**: Early computer networks like ARPANET and Cold War requirements birthed fundamental security models. The Biba model prioritizes data integrity (preventing data corruption via reading up and writing down), while the Bell-LaPadula model prioritizes confidentiality (preventing data leakage via writing up and reading down). Cold War systems enforced Mandatory Access Control (MAC) and multi-level security—exemplified historically by the IBM AS/400 (now iSeries)—alongside human data custodians who vetted, extracted, and printed authorized records on green-bar paper.
- **The Modern Shift & Cloud Risks**: Rapid business demands, pervasive API access, cloud migrations, mobile laptops, and high-capacity flash storage dismantled structured repositories. Hoy notes that organizations often move unclassified, unstructured data directly into public Amazon S3 instances or decentralized Hadoop clusters without evaluating exposure.
- **Flaws in the Data Security Lifecycle**: Standard cloud security lifecycles frequently omit two essential safeguards: retention policies and verified backups. Hoy emphasizes that data hoarders retaining decades of old email archives (PST files) represent massive liabilities in a breach, pointing to the Sony hack as an example. Furthermore, unverified backups leave systems helpless against ransomware.

### Technical Details & Implementation
- **Data Classification as the Core Foundation**: Relying solely on eDiscovery scanning across petabytes of unstructured data is compared to trying to clean up a flood with a wet/dry vac—scanning is simply too slow and resource-heavy. Instead, organizations must require end users to tag and classify documents at the point of creation. Because data aggregates like water, tracking newly classified files leads security teams directly to repositories where high-value data resides.
- **People, Processes, and Technology**: Effective governance requires executive buy-in, clear data retention rules, and user accountability (including termination for attempting to game classification). On the technology front, Hoy discusses machine learning/pattern-based classification metadata tagging, eDiscovery, CASB tools, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP). He stresses that DLP is ineffective if set only to monitor and alert; it must actively block data exfiltration, supported by classification tags to minimize business-disrupting false positives.
- **Architectural Controls**: Hoy advocates for defensive architecture such as isolating sensitive data within Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environments, enforcing tight Access Control Lists (ACLs), multi-factor authentication at internal choke points, deploying rights management and encryption, and poisoning exfiltrated documents using canary techniques like honeydocs. He also notes User Behavior Analytics (UBA) can record suspicious actions when employees attempt to circumvent security controls.

### Takeaways
Hoy concludes that attackers often know where the crown jewels are better than the victims do, making it unforgivable to leave internal networks wide open. Organizations cannot protect or govern what they do not know they have. Before attempting complex frameworks like Carnegie Mellon's CMMI Data Management Maturity (DMM) model, enterprises must master basic data classification, enforce strict data destruction/retention policies, ensure reliable backups, restrict risky users to locked-down VDI sessions, and configure defensive technologies to actively block unauthorized movement.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - How to Security Research Without Getting Sucked into a Courtroom (Robert Adams)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of LayerOne 2018 - How to Security Research Without Getting Sucked into a Courtroom (Robert Adams).
talks.summary:
Overview
Robert Adams, a licensed attorney specializing in cybersecurity law, explains how security researchers can conduct technical research without legal consequences. The talk covers federal statutes, criminal versus civil liability, and practical protective measures.

Key Topics
The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 USC §1030) is central to the discussion. Adams distinguishes between five relevant sections: §1030(a)(1) prohibits unauthorized access to U.S. government computers with no intent requirement (accidental violations possible); §1030(a)(2) requires intentional unauthorized access to obtain "information" (broadly defined, creating ambiguity about what constitutes illegal data theft); §1030(a)(5)(a) targets malware creators who knowingly transmit code causing intentional damage; and critically, §1030(a)(5)(c)—the "fuck-you clause" for researchers—makes it illegal to intentionally access a system where that access causes any damage or loss, regardless of whether damage was intended. The term "protected computer" is extremely broad, covering federal systems and any system affecting interstate or foreign commerce, encompassing nearly all modern computers.

The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (17 USC §1201) prohibits circumventing technological measures controlling access to works, applying to authentication handshakes, code signing, and protocol encryption.

Adams emphasizes the distinction between the U.S. legal system and justice system: courts determine what can be proven, not what is fair. He addresses defamation risks, noting that truth is a defense and researchers should stick to factual statements with supporting evidence rather than opinions or assumptions. First Amendment protection exists for speech but not freedom from consequences; prior restraints on speech violate the First Amendment except in narrow contexts like national security or illegal content.

Technical Details and Protections
To avoid §1030(a)(5)(c) violations, Adams recommends: adding detailed code comments documenting intent; implementing request throttling to limit server impact; researching target infrastructure (hosting location, pricing model) to assess potential costs from access; and avoiding generating excessive traffic that could constitute measurable damage or loss.

For vulnerability disclosure, Adams strongly advises never requesting payment (extortion/blackmail risk), though accepting offered bounties is acceptable. He recommends conducting disclosure through an attorney rather than directly, allowing attorney-client privilege to shield identity and creating legal buffer against injunctive relief attempts.

Other protections include screenshotting evidence, staying informed about state-specific laws, obtaining and understanding liability insurance exclusions (many exclude unpatched systems), and understanding that once banned from a system, returning constitutes intentional access, nearly guaranteeing CFAA violation.

Criminal Procedure
If arrested, Adams advises: comply with lawful orders without resistance; provide only name, address, and birthdate; immediately request an attorney; cease all questioning if an attorney is requested; and avoid providing any information through seemingly innocent questions, as even minor statements can incriminate.

Civil Liability
Under CFAA §1030(g), companies can sue for compensatory damages or injunctive relief. Compensatory damages cover direct costs; consequential damages include labor, server replacement, backup restoration, and increased operational costs (especially for cloud-hosted systems charged per transaction). A two-year statute of limitations applies from discovery, not access. A "negligent design" clause provides defense if code comments demonstrate unintended behavior.

Takeaways
Security research operates within a legal framework with significant gray areas. Researchers must understand that access-based liability depends on system impact, not intent to damage. Practical measures—documentation, throttling, legal counsel—substantially reduce risk. The legal system rewards those who can prove their actions and intentions; detailed code comments and evidence collection are defensive essentials. Using an attorney as intermediary for disclosure provides substantial protection through privilege and shifts legal exposure away from the researcher.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - Git for Hackers (RtzqO)
talks.teaser: Explains why deleted secrets survive in git repositories, and how git's internals keep old commits and objects recoverable.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why removing sensitive data from a git repository is much harder than it seems. It opens with a search of public GitHub commits titled as deletions of private keys, where the speaker found around 77,821 such commits, to show how often credentials are left behind in public history. He then walks through git's internal model of blobs, trees, commits and references, all stored as objects addressed by SHA-1 hashes.

Using a very small example repository, the talk demonstrates the common ways a deletion fails. Removing a file and committing leaves the old objects in place. A filter-branch rewrite creates new commits but keeps the originals. Garbage collection packs objects into pack files, and the reflog keeps old references for a default period, so a commit can survive a gc until the reflog and packed refs are cleaned up by hand. Git notes, stored under their own references and mostly hidden in hosting interfaces, can keep text attached to commits on deleted branches.

The closing section covers how to examine a repository found in the wild: unpack the pack files, inflate every object and scan it for credentials, and check that scanning tools really find what they should. The main advice is to stop secrets reaching the repository in the first place, through repository-side checks, code review and proper credential management, since local pre-commit hooks are hard to enforce across a team.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - HTTP2 and You (Security Panda)
talks.teaser: Explains HTTP/2 basics, surveys its real-world deployment, and shows how to find and test servers using it at scale.
talks.summary:
HTTP/2 was published in 2015 as RFC 7540 and is now widely deployed, yet the speaker argues that security researchers still focus mostly on HTTP/1.1. The protocol is binary rather than text, uses multiplexed streams, compresses headers with HPACK, supports server push, and negotiates the protocol during TLS through ALPN. The talk also covers the tooling gap: few proxies can record HTTP/2 traffic, so testers often rely on browser developer tools, online checkers, command-line clients, Burp, or Wireshark.

To measure adoption, the speaker ran masscan across about 49 million addresses listening on port 443, then used nmap scripts on those hosts, which took over a week and found roughly 300,000 HTTP/2 instances. Shodan snapshots showed growth from about 2.3 million sites in February to about 3.6 million a couple of months later, with nginx the leading product. Scanning also turned up weaknesses: a slow-read denial-of-service issue on about 7,000 Apache systems out of a million scanned, and HPACK decompression bombs and priority-based attacks on a much smaller number of hosts. Cloud hosting was a practical hurdle, since Google Cloud eventually banned the researcher's account after repeated compliance reviews, while a cheaper VPS provider was more tolerant of scanning.

For defenders, the recommendations are to patch and keep servers current, disable HTTP/2 where it is not needed, rate-limit requests and connections, and use stricter timeouts, because some servers keep connections open by default. The speaker said a second part would cover misconfigurations and pointed to implementation lists and the RFC as reference material.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - Adware is Just Malware (Amit Serper)
talks.teaser: Traces a macOS adware family through its install scripts, persistence tricks and browser hijacking tactics.
talks.summary:
The talk follows up on a Mac adware family the speaker first analyzed two years earlier. After an update broke a removal script written earlier, the speaker returned to new samples and found much of the earlier code reused. The adware arrives through installers from third-party download sites. Each stage fetches the next payload, and watchdog components restore anything that gets removed. Random names drawn from a word list make infections hard to compare.

The analysis showed a root-level install script that relies on the password a user types into the installer, since the account is usually in the sudoers list. A later binary reports a machine identifier to a remote server and runs commands through a shell. Ad-hoc code signing was used to slip past some checks, and browser detection decided which ad packages to fetch. The final stage used AppleScript to inject JavaScript into browsers, rewriting search pages and displaying ads. Attribution rested on a username left in archive metadata, matching script functions and debug strings, and a domain registered without privacy protection.

The takeaway is that installers from unofficial sites can act like malware before any license screen appears, and that code signing does not prove safety. Defenders should check launch agents, launch daemons and browser settings directly, since the speaker argued that common Mac security tools miss these persistence methods. The company named in the samples answered with legal letters, which the speaker also covered.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018 - Raise Me: Resume Workshop
talks.teaser: Hands-on resume and interview strategies show how career changers can land roles in information security despite conventional HR filters.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how standardized HR job requisitions favor checklist candidates yet undermine the diverse backgrounds strong engineering teams need. The speaker, a seasoned hiring manager who is re-entering information security, cites industry shortage data and distinguishes full career pivots from moving into a new security specialty or an internal role change.

For hiring managers, the talk argues that career changers can fill stubborn openings, ramp like juniors without junior baggage, and bring fresh documentation and certification energy. For candidates, a four-part path covers building qualifications through current-job stretch work, consulting, volunteer disaster-response projects, speaking, open source, competitions, and certifications matched to target postings; rejecting resume blitzes and buzzword padding; maintaining a master resume and tailoring essay-style targeted versions that answer each requirement; and interviewing with prepared thirty-second answers while negotiating realistically when stepping back to move forward.

The session ties these ideas to the Raise Me career-development effort at SCALE and ends with brief recruiting pitches from several employers, then shifts to a resume workshop exercise for attendees who brought materials.

talks.title: LayerOne 2018
talks.teaser: Experienced practitioners share practical guidance on breaking into infosec, hiring, and career growth.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the idea that there is no single path into security and that curiosity about how technology works matters more than a prescribed degree. Panelists describe common entry routes through system or network administration, software development, embedded work, SOC roles, and consultancy, and they stress long-term planning while acknowledging that hiring norms have shifted so newcomers can sometimes land security roles sooner when they show real skill.

Discussion turns to what hiring managers want: honesty about gaps, persistence, communication when delivering bad news, teamwork, and genuine enthusiasm for the field rather than box-checking for a paycheck. They compare certifications as resume filters versus proof of ability, recommend hands-on practice through CTFs, guided labs, Linux fluency, conferences, and networking, and debate whether vulnerable VMs alone suffice without structured training for beginners.

Audience questions cover client-facing soft skills, builder versus breaker balance, tools such as Kali and Parrot, paths toward pen testing and forensics, chain of custody, advancing toward executive roles, cross-training, and how accounting or other backgrounds map to audit, forensics, or internal roles. The panel closes by encouraging smaller employers for breadth, corporate experience for scale, and matching opportunities to personality rather than a single industry template.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - The Hotel Room Gourmet (Deviant Ollam & Pinup)
talks.teaser: Attendees learn hotel-room sous-vide setups, road shopping lists, and drink pairings for eating well between security events.
talks.summary:
Security travelers often default to convention food and bar menus, which leaves little control over calories, cost, or enjoyment. The session opens with that liberty-minded framing: choosing what goes into your body matters as much on the road as at home, and conference life does not have to mean stale pizza or skipped meals.

The core demo walks through a repeatable hotel workflow. Shop the perimeter of a grocery store for eggs, steak, cheese, butter, and produce; request a fridge when needed; and cook with gear that fits luggage. Sous-vide in buckets or coolers holds meat at precise temperatures for hours, then a cast-iron pan, induction plate, or Searzall finishes the Maillard crust. The audience tastes pork, cheese, and ribeye prepared that way while hearing practical details on seasoning, bag choice, stacking cooks by temperature, and a portable cocktail kit for drinks like Sazeracs.

Takeaway: assemble a small road kitchen, batch egg custards in jars, and treat cooking as practice with “infinite continues” rather than a specialty skill. Slides and shopping lists are promised online; egg cups finish in a chill-out room after the session.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - SMTP Security in a Changing World (Katie Knowles)
talks.teaser: Traces how SMTP grew from an open mail relay to SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and the standards fights behind them.
talks.summary:
The talk traces SMTP from its plain-text beginnings in the early 1980s, when two servers greet each other and pass a message. Later additions brought STARTTLS encryption, authentication before relaying, and the closing of open relays. The core problem is that the envelope sender and the sender a recipient sees are separate fields, so a message can claim a domain it never came from.

The middle covers the standards that followed. SPF lets a domain publish a DNS list of servers allowed to send for it, with actions such as soft fail or hard fail. DKIM signs messages with a private key, but a domain cannot state what should happen when a signature fails. DMARC, formally published in 2015, ties SPF and DKIM together through alignment with the visible sender, sets a none, quarantine or reject policy, can apply it to a chosen percentage of failing mail, and sends aggregate and forensic reports. Sender ID, a Microsoft-backed rival, is now defunct in the speaker's view.

The speaker's advice is to publish DMARC with a policy of none at first, which collects feedback without affecting delivery. Adoption among large providers is under 10%, and the speaker noted that open-source tools for parsing the XML feedback are scarce. The talk closes on a hopeful note: email can be rethought, and recent messaging apps show what newer designs might look like.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - Getting off The Grid and onto Hyperboria (William Turner)
talks.teaser: Explains mesh networking and the Hyperborea network, showing how to join it and what it still lacks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by contrasting the textbook definition of a mesh network, where every node connects to every other, with how these networks behave in practice. The speaker surveys long-running mesh technologies such as Batman, OLSR, ZigBee and Z-Wave, then turns to Hyperborea, a wide area network that runs on the CJDNS routing layer and had around 1,500 nodes at the time. Peering used to depend on trusted contacts who exchanged keys, and the speaker notes that auto-peering discovery now exists alongside community lists of public peers.

The middle of the talk is a walkthrough of joining the network. A user builds CJDNS, edits the configuration file it generates, and connects to a public peer, which the speaker warns is often out of date. A command-line client then lets the user ping nodes, trace routes, list peers and read traffic statistics through the local admin interface. Node addresses derive from each node's public key, and the IPv6 range used sits in a private block, so the network does not interfere with the public internet. The speaker then reviews the services layered on top: content-addressed file sharing through IPFS, several decentralized DNS options backed by blockchains, and blockchain-based storage projects that pay providers. For each, the speaker explains the trade-offs, such as the cost of offering storage and the lack of a default caching layer.

The talk closes with a practical point: Hyperborea still lacks DNS, publishable storage, out-of-band node management and any governance model for misbehaving nodes. The speaker describes a Los Angeles group forming to build a city-scale mesh for emergency communications and to win support from local officials. The main takeaway for practitioners is that tooling and governance remain the open problems, and that the aim is to connect people rather than hardware.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - How Containers Contain (z0rro)
talks.teaser: Walks through the Linux primitives behind containers: chroot, namespaces, cgroups and capabilities, with live demos.
talks.summary:
This talk is a high-level tour of the Linux building blocks that container frameworks such as Docker, LXC and systemd-nspawn rely on. Containers share the host's kernel rather than virtualizing hardware or another operating system, so they are best understood as processes kept apart from the rest of the machine. The first building block covered is chroot, which changes the apparent root directory for a group of processes. A demo copied a binary and its library dependencies into a separate directory and ran the command there.

Kernel namespaces came next, isolating things such as mount points, process IDs, networking, IPC, hostnames and users. Using unshare to start a process with its own PID and mount namespaces, the speaker showed that the process was the only one visible inside. User namespaces were highlighted as especially important for security, because root inside a container maps to an unprivileged user ID on the host. Control groups were shown limiting and accounting for resources such as CPU shares and memory. In one demo, an nginx process placed in a memory-limited cgroup was killed once it went over its allowance.

Capabilities split root privileges into finer-grained grants. Using setcap, the speaker gave nginx only the ability to bind a privileged port, so it could run as a non-root user. The speaker warned that some capabilities, such as CAP_SYS_ADMIN, have a history of container escapes and should be granted sparingly. systemd-nspawn was presented as a lightweight option, though not one the speaker would call production-ready by default. The practical advice was to confirm that a framework uses user namespaces and to trim unneeded capabilities. seccomp, SELinux and AppArmor were mentioned but left for other talks.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of LayerOne 2017 - Exploiting USB/IP in Linux (Ignat Korchagin).
talks.summary:
### Overview
At LayerOne 2017, Ignat (an engineer at Cloudflare) presented on the inner workings and security implications of USB/IP in Linux, specifically detailing a remote vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-3955 (nicknamed "u-boat"). USB/IP is a technology designed to forward USB Request Blocks (URBs) over a TCP network connection, enabling a client machine to import and manage physical USB devices attached to an exporting server. Ignat demonstrated how architectural design decisions in the Linux implementation—specifically delegating network protocol parsing directly to the kernel—resulted in a critical remote heap buffer overflow.

### Key Topics
- **USB/IP Architecture:** A client-server model where an exporter server runs `usbipd` alongside kernel drivers (`usbip-core`, `usbip-host`/stub driver), and an importing client uses a user-space utility, `usbip-core`, and the Virtual Host Controller Interface (`vhci-hcd`) driver.
- **Kernel-Level Protocol Handling:** Unlike standard Linux VPN architectures that follow the "tools in kernel, policy in user space" paradigm using tun/tap devices and userland daemons, USB/IP passes the TCP socket file descriptor directly to kernel space after initial negotiation, executing full application-layer protocol parsing in ring 0.
- **Vulnerability Mechanics (CVE-2016-3955):** In the client receiving path, packet header parsing extracts payload length into URB metadata without verifying whether the target URB transfer buffer is sufficiently large before pulling the rest of the payload off the socket, resulting in an arbitrary-length heap buffer overflow.
- **Exploitation and SLUB Manipulation:** Leveraging SLUB cache allocations to turn a denial-of-service crash into potential arbitrary kernel code execution or data tampering.

### Technical Details
In a standard USB/IP workflow, a client negotiates device import via TCP with the server's daemon. Once successful, the socket descriptor is handed to the kernel `vhci-hcd` driver. When handling incoming packets, the kernel parses the USB/IP header directly into an internal kernel `urb` structure, storing the payload length into a variable (`size`) and immediately receiving that amount of data into `urb->transfer_buffer`. Because standard USB host drivers allocate fixed-size transfer buffers (assuming benign hardware that never returns more data than requested during enumeration or driver operations), an unvalidated network payload allows an attacker to write arbitrary bytes past buffer boundaries.

Ignat demonstrated this attack using an Ubuntu machine running a vulnerable vanilla 4.4.8 kernel. By running a rogue user-space USB/IP server written in Go (running on an unprivileged port above 1024), the server advertised a fake device (vendor/product ID `0xdeadbeef`). When the client attempted device enumeration (expecting a 64-byte response), the server returned 576 bytes, corrupting kernel heap memory and triggering a kernel crash. Because an attacker controls URB responses and can emulate arbitrary USB device profiles (which trigger `udev` to load specific drivers allocating in desired SLUB caches like `kmalloc-32`, `kmalloc-64`, etc.), an attacker can systematically direct which SLUB cache to target, significantly easing reliable kernel heap exploitation beyond single-chunk corruption limits.

### Takeaways
To mitigate these risks, users should:
1. Reconsider using USB/IP unless strictly necessary, especially for inexpensive hardware.
2. Keep Linux kernels patched, as USB/IP kernel modules in modern distributions are maintained in mainline.
3. Wrap all USB/IP network communications in authenticated and encrypted tunnels (such as TLS), because USB/IP natively lacks encryption, authentication, or tamper protection, leaving it vulnerable to MITM attacks or rogue servers capable of spoofing malicious devices (e.g., keyboards or monitors).
