talks.title: LayerOne 2017
talks.teaser: Practical guidance ties attacker intent, capability, and opportunity to risks in home, mobile, corporate, and industrial setups.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by arguing that effective threat modeling is mostly disciplined common sense rather than heavyweight vendor methodologies or card games. He stresses that much of the Internet still runs on obscurity and half-fixes, that logical flaws often matter more than exotic zero-days, and that defenders should plan for likely eventualities instead of every hypothetical nightmare.

The core of the session walks through high-level threat and risk sketches for personal home networks, mobile devices and carrier-side weaknesses, corporate workstations, security appliances that bridge or bypass firewalls, and embedded or industrial gear including SCADA and publicly exposed SMB. Examples include mass MS17-010 exposure, leaked offensive toolkits, SS7-style routing abuse, FireEye-style appliance compromise paths, and a fictional unpatched mining-control device that must accept inbound vendor access.

Closing advice emphasizes realistic attitude, enforced egress and segmentation choke points, treating appliances as untrusted computers, and resisting hype-driven panic or “unhackable” marketing. Nation-state operators still phone home over ordinary networks, so logging boundary failures and thinking briefly like an attacker often surfaces gaps that paperwork misses. Q&A reinforces that painful outages usually trace to refused patches, forgotten ACLs, or business pressure overriding basic hygiene.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - Turning Joy into Sadness: Common Cryptography Anti-Patterns (Becker Polverini)
talks.teaser: A consultant walks through real password, cipher-mode, and MAC failures from audits and names safer libraries and algorithms to reach for.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by reframing “don’t roll your own crypto”: teams still must assemble standard primitives for logins, blob encryption, and protocol key material, and that glue is where many products fail. Examples come from consulting rescues, including Stack Overflow–style recipes that chain Base64, fast hashes, weak salting, and unsafe comparison patterns.

Password storage is traced from naive hashing through salted MD5-style schemes, iterated fast hashes, and hand-built PBKDF-like loops that leak timing and length behavior—including a constant-time equality check that validated empty strings. The speaker argues for memory-hard password hashes such as scrypt and Argon2, HKDF for stretching shared secrets, and constant-time equality helpers from mature libraries. Block cipher misuse covers ECB’s visual leakage, why CBC and counter mode alone are insufficient, and authenticated encryption; a counter-mode JSON field flip turned withdraw/deposit semantics in a financial audit. MAC discussion explains length-extension on Merkle–Damgård designs, why HMAC-on-SHA-1 is treacherous, and why SHA-3 aligns better with keyed hashing intuition.

Closing guidance favors libsodium-style stacks: ChaCha20-Poly1305 for AEAD, Argon2 for passwords, SHA-3 for digests and HMAC, and modern curves near 255-bit security for asymmetric work, with brief Q&A on JavaScript comparisons, NIST curves, AES performance, and transport alternatives.

talks.title: LayerOne 2017 - From Zero to Bender in 12 Months (Zapp & Hyr0n)
talks.teaser: Charts a software developer's year-long path from Arduino kits to mass-producing hackable DEF CON conference badges.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe how a middleware software engineer with no real hardware background set out to build the Bender badge for DEF CON 24 as a side project with the AND!XOR group. Starting after DEF CON 23, the path ran through Arduino starter kits, learning solder and KiCad, breadboard prototypes, and a long chain of revisions where USB, reset, displays, and radios repeatedly failed until a shippable design emerged.

The talk spends substantial time on lessons from scaling up: BOM cost pressure near six thousand dollars for the first run, hand-placing on the order of ten thousand components, roughly fifty percent yield, solder bridges, brown-bounce ground issues killing RF, and sharing one SPI bus between radio, display, and flash. The follow-on DEF CON 25 badge (Bender Thompson) moves to a Nordic BMD300 module, color LCD, WS2812 LEDs, MacroFab assembly, preprocessed SD assets, dual SPI buses, and a custom driver reaching about twenty-two frames per second, plus Chip8 emulation and a small on-badge scripting layer.

Takeaways emphasize running design rule checks before Gerbers, matching parts to fab processes, investing in test gear when RF or power misbehaves, treating Arduino as a gateway into bare-metal toolchains, and picking a motivating community project if the goal is to learn hardware well enough to manufacture and repair hundreds of hackable badges.

talks.title: LayerOne 2016 - Hacking Commercial ATMs and Safes (XCC & Alex)
talks.teaser: Researchers demonstrate BLE replay, keypad sniffing, and lock-body brute force against commercial ATM-style electronic safes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with UL burglary and tool-resistance ratings for commercial safes and electronic locks, then walks through well-known physical and skimming attacks on ATMs and safes before focusing on a specific keypad and lock body the team purchased and tested, including default manager and user codes on a six-digit lock.

Wireless analysis with Bluetooth Low Energy capture gear shows advertising and connection behavior, a likely stack issue, and replayable unlock packets where only checksum and signal strength change between attempts. Reverse engineering the Android app exposes stored lock state and addresses, and shows the unlock path sending the PIN as a reversed long integer while unused encryption routines sit in the codebase. A demo captures an unlock and surfaces the entered manager code.

Teardown and logic-analyzer work on the four-wire keypad-to-lock link decode an 8-bit protocol and show that pin-check logic lives in the entry pad, not only in the certified lock body. The presenters replay unlock traffic with an Arduino, brute force the lock body, and summarize risks such as BLE wardriving, knowing when a safe is open, keypad implants, and cable tapping. They close with cautions for high-security deployments and opinions on extending UL testing to cover communications and encryption.

talks.title: Dr Tran - Insurance for your Cyber
talks.teaser: Explains how insurers price cyber breach policies, what they cover, and which exclusions and application answers buyers should check.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how insurance works in general, from ancient merchants sharing cargo losses through premiums, underwriting and claims. It notes that insurers often earn more from investing premiums than from the premiums themselves, which is why their pricing depends on detailed historical data. The speaker then turns to the newer market of cyber breach policies, where coverage differs widely from one insurer to another. Examples of what a policy may pay for include regulatory defense, forensic response, customer credit monitoring and extortion payments.

The middle section describes how cyber underwriting is still rudimentary, relying on yes-or-no application questions about antivirus, card-payment compliance and recent penetration tests, which show only a point in time. Figures cited include roughly two billion dollars in annual cyber premiums, against an estimated 85 billion dollar global market and 1 billion dollars in 2013, compared with a 48 billion dollar US auto policy market. A recent case in which an insurer sued a customer over an inaccurate application answer about network monitoring shows why answers must match reality.

The closing advice is that security staff should take part when risk management and finance teams complete applications, and that companies should read exclusions carefully and decide whether coverage is really needed. The speaker suggests insurers ask about incident response speed and collect consistent breach data, and notes that current information sharing is siloed and not very actionable. The overall takeaway is that the market is immature and buyers should know exactly what they are purchasing.

talks.title: Chi Barnett - The Ethical Spy
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Chi Barnett - The Ethical Spy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Chi Barnett, a data scientist working in home automation (with previous experience at Tinder), discusses the critical balance between building useful data-driven services and preserving user privacy. Modern applications like recommendation engines and crowdsourced traffic tools (such as Waze) require extensive user data to function effectively, but accidental or intentional disclosures can introduce severe real-world physical and safety risks. Barnett argues that existing privacy policies fail because they are written in opaque legalese aimed at protecting service providers rather than empowering users. To address this, Barnett proposes establishing a formal voluntary standard—currently being developed as an IETF draft—modeled on medical informed consent to govern data collection, disclosure, and lifecycle management.

### Key Topics
- **The Medical Informed Consent Model**: Borrowing from medical law, Barnett outlines the three fundamental pillars required for legitimate consent:
  1. *Disclosure*: Users must clearly understand what data is collected and how it will be used.
  2. *Capacity*: The user must be capable of understanding risk and exercising autonomy (referencing age standards such as 13 under COPPA, or legal incapacitation).
  3. *Voluntariness*: Consent cannot be coerced through force or undue pressure where the user cannot practically say no.
- **Utilities vs. Non-Utilities**: The standard distinguishes standard services from entities that function as utilities (services like the electric company or potential future mandatory transit platforms). When opting out would cause severe negative life consequences, mandatory data collection is inherently coercive. Therefore, utilities should only be permitted to require essential billing details (such as a billing address, which can be bypassed via electronic payment), making all other data collection optional.
- **Mandatory vs. Optional Metrics**: Services can define metrics as mandatory only if they are strictly required for core functionality (e.g., location pings for real-time routing in Waze or Lyft). Value-added features (e.g., long-term search history) and data collection for future unannounced innovations must be treated as optional with explicit opt-out mechanisms that clearly state what functionality degrades if declined.
- **Lifecycle Disclosures and Third-Party Sharing**: Disclosures must cover the entire data lifecycle: collection, usage, retention duration, security/encryption models, destruction plans, and breach response policies. If data is shared with third parties, the receiving party's retention, security, and privacy terms must also be disclosed.
- **Capacity Loss and Retroactive Opt-Outs**: If a user becomes incapacitated or dies, a designated proxy should manage consent; otherwise, consent is treated as withdrawn. When minors or incapacitated users are found to have consented invalidly, data must be purged immediately. Furthermore, user opt-outs should be retroactive by default, purging previously collected data.

### Technical Details
- **Draft Format**: Barnett authored the initial IETF draft using XML intended for conversion to standard RFC text format using the IETF XML conversion tool.
- **Data Categorization**: The framework distinguishes *content* (data meant for human consumption) from *metrics* (machine-readable data used by the service, such as clickstreams or demographic tags), as well as differentiating non-sensitive data, sensitive data, and legally defined Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
- **Alarm Fatigue & Default Opt-Outs**: To combat user notification fatigue from constant disclosure updates, providers may opt to treat features as opt-out by default from inception while providing minimal core functionality.

### Takeaways
Barnett emphasizes that establishing trust requires enforceable accountability, standardized templated disclosure language, and clear risk communication (such as reminding users that retained data is subject to government subpoenas). The speaker invites community collaboration from attendees to refine the draft into an actionable standard.

talks.title: Jos Weyers - Showing Keys in Public (What Could Possibly Go Wrong?)
talks.teaser: A lock picker walks through how photos of keys in public enable duplication via decoding, molding, and social engineering.
talks.summary:
Physical keys act like passwords: anyone who learns the bitting can copy them. The presentation opens with sport lock picking ethics, then surveys real services and stunts that turn smartphone photos or mailed images into working duplicates, including insurance marketing that 3D-scans keys on a pedestal.

Case studies span distant lens photos of Quickset keys, blurred conference shots of widely shared handcuff keys, social-engineered mailbox photos used to laser-cut a hackerspace door key, news broadcasts that display subway and fire-service master keys, and Belgian speed-camera keys decoded from video frames. The speaker also demonstrates low-tech clay molds and casting for brief access to unattended keys, plus products and social feeds that invite owners to publish key images.

The closing argument treats key exposure like shouting a PIN in a crowd: lose sight of a key for roughly twenty seconds and treat it as compromised. Practitioners should assume watchers with phones, CCTV, or long lenses, refuse to broadcast credentials, and weigh safety-driven master-key distribution against the inability to keep secrets among thousands of holders.

talks.title: Viss - How Not to InfoSec
talks.teaser: Catalogues avoidable security blunders, from plaintext passwords to ignored disclosures, with the lesson drawn from each.
talks.summary:
This talk is a catalogue of avoidable security mistakes, framed as "what not to do" cautionary tales rather than step-by-step advice. The speaker argues that showing failures helps an audience narrow down good decisions by elimination. Early examples cover a company that intercepted encrypted web traffic for advertising, vendors that shipped software which logged keystrokes or installed DRM code on customers' machines, and a network team that ran gear near full session capacity and then blocked scanning of it.

The middle section moves through cases where basic hygiene failed. Passwords were kept in plain text in mailboxes, OneNote files and spreadsheets, and a company file share readable by everyone held credentials alongside personal and financial records. Reused passwords let a tool such as Mimikatz move from one workstation into a production domain. Long-running servers were left unpatched for years, and a set of switches went down together after an old memory leak. A security analyst was seen deleting thousands of alerts unreviewed each day. A digital sign with default credentials exposed a large LED billboard in Georgia, and the speaker says the vendor largely ignored the earlier disclosure. Pen-test mistakes are also covered, such as scanners that broke web applications and brute forcing that locked user accounts.

The closing part covers public response to breaches. The speaker recommends honest statements, prepared incident response notes, and treating reported problems seriously. The main takeaway is that real security work happens in configuration and code, not in documents.
